Images, signal-to-noise, moving-object detection, and artifact rejection.
Sky position, timing, orbit fitting, covariance, and impact probability.
Brightness, albedo, spectra, rotation, size, and composition.
Range, delay, velocity, momentum transfer, and independent orbit constraints.
Energy, atmospheric entry, fragmentation, consequence uncertainty, and deflection physics.
Completeness, observing geometry, response decisions, communication, and long-term readiness.
Survey Imaging Lead
Distinguishes real moving sources from cosmic rays, detector defects, and image-processing artifacts using repeated and independent observations.
How does Nguyen separate a real moving object from a detector artefact?
It appears in independent exposures and moves consistently
Artefacts are always brighter on the frame than a real detection is
Real objects appear on only one detector at a time
Cosmic rays are removed by the telescope's own software
Orbit Determination Lead
Treats every position as a timed measurement with calibration and covariance, then asks which observation reduces the dangerous uncertainty.
Why does Rossi treat a position as a timed measurement rather than a point?
An orbit is fitted to when as much as where
A position is only valid for the night on which it was taken
Timing decides which telescope gets credit for the observation
The covariance is computed from exposure length
Physical Characterization Lead
Combines brightness, color, spectra, thermal information, and rotation without pretending any one observable uniquely determines size or composition.
Why will Adebayo not give a diameter from brightness alone?
Brightness is size and reflectivity together
Brightness cannot be measured accurately at the faintest magnitudes
Diameter requires a radar detection by definition
Reflectivity is the same for every asteroid of a given type
Radar Dynamics Lead
Uses signal delay and Doppler measurements to add independent geometric constraints to optical astrometry.
What does radar add that optical astrometry cannot give?
A direct distance and line-of-sight speed
A far more accurate measurement of the very same position on the sky
The object's composition from the returned frequency
Observations that can be made in daylight
Impact Physics Lead
Connects size, density, speed, atmosphere, and fragmentation to consequence ranges rather than single deterministic outcomes.
Why does Banerjee give consequence as a range rather than a number?
Three uncertain inputs multiply through the calculation
A range is required by protocol before any public statement is made
Deterministic answers are only possible after entry
The range describes how likely an impact is
Survey and Response Lead
Balances observing completeness, uncertainty reduction, public communication, and response thresholds without confusing expected value with a prediction.
What is Garcia guarding against when she says expected value is not a prediction?
A tiny chance of something enormous gives a number nobody will see
Expected value cannot be computed before the orbit is known
Probabilities below one per cent are not meaningful to a general audience
The public always misreads percentages
Survey Pipeline Scientist

Owns the software that decides which of the night's forty thousand detections
a human being ever sees. Most of what it flags is a satellite, a cosmic ray or
a column of hot pixels.

Her measure of the pipeline is not how many objects it finds but how many real
ones it throws away, which can only be known by feeding it synthetic objects
and counting how many come back.
How does Virtanen measure whether the survey is missing objects?
By planting known objects and seeing how many are found
By comparing the number found this year with last year
By checking that no uncatalogued objects appear in the catalogue
By observing the same field twice on the same night
Astrometrist

Turns images into positions, which sounds mechanical and is where most orbit
errors are actually born. A position is only as good as the star catalogue it
was measured against and the clock that timestamped it.

He looks for structure in residuals across the focal plane. A bias that grows
toward the corner of a detector is an instrument problem wearing the costume
of an orbital one.
What does Delacroix conclude from residuals that grow toward one corner of the detector?
The error follows position on the detector, not the sky
The object is accelerating in a way gravity does not explain
The exposure times were recorded in the wrong time standard
The telescope was tracking at the wrong rate
Thermal Infrared Observer

Measures asteroids in the infrared, where what is seen is heat the body
re-radiates rather than sunlight it reflects. That breaks the tie between a
small bright object and a large dark one.

Reflected light alone gives brightness, which is the product of size and
reflectivity. Two unknowns, one measurement — and every consequence estimate
downstream cubes whichever size you guessed.
Why does Sorokin's infrared measurement pin down a diameter that optical brightness cannot?
Thermal emission depends on size and temperature, not reflectivity
Infrared telescopes have better angular resolution
Reflected light cannot be measured for faint objects
The infrared band is unaffected by distance
Radar Astronomer

Transmits at an asteroid and listens for the echo, which is the only method in
this campaign that measures a distance directly instead of inferring it.

The catch is geometry. Radar strength falls with the fourth power of distance,
so the technique that collapses an orbit works for a few days per apparition
and then not at all for years.
Why is a radar window so short and so valuable?
The returned signal weakens as the fourth power of range
The transmitter overheats after a few hours of use
Radar requires the object to be in the Earth's shadow
Other observatories are booked for optical work at exactly the same hours
Impact Physics Modeller

Models what happens between the top of the atmosphere and the ground, where
an object either arrives intact, breaks up and deposits its energy as a burst,
or does something in between.

Which of those happens depends on the body's strength, and strength is the
quantity nobody has measured for the object in question. Her models therefore
produce distributions, and she resists every request to reduce one to a
headline number.
Why do Schulz's entry models produce a range of outcomes rather than one?
The body's strength is unmeasured, and it decides whether it fragments
Atmospheric density at those heights is never known to better than a factor of two
The models are run on different computers with different rounding
Entry angle cannot be determined before impact
Preparedness Coordinator

Translates a probability that keeps moving into actions that people can take
without being made fools of when it moves again.

Her tool is the pre-agreed trigger: what has to be observed, by when, for a
given protective step to begin. Announced in advance, it survives a
probability that falls; announced afterwards, it looks like improvisation.
Why does Ellery agree protective triggers before the probability settles?
A step tied to a stated observation survives the probability changing
Triggers reduce the uncertainty in the orbit determination
Regulations require evacuation plans to be filed in advance
Announcing them early is what stops the media reporting the risk badly
The fraction of incident light a surface reflects.
Measurement of an object position on the sky.
The average Earth–Sun distance, about 150 million kilometres. Orbit sizes are quoted in it.
The correction between what an instrument reads and what is true, established against something known.
A description of how uncertainties in fitted quantities vary together.
A table of where an object will be, night by night, computed from its orbit. Its uncertainty is what a telescope has to search.
Brightness measured as a function of time.
The apparent shift of an object against the background stars when the observer moves. With a known baseline it gives a distance by triangle.
Measuring how light is polarised after reflection, which constrains what a surface is made of and how rough it is.
Round-trip travel time of a radar signal, used to infer range.
The angular separation between an object and the Sun as seen from the observer.
The Discovery Image
Validate a new-object candidate and preserve the measurements needed for follow-up.
A survey telescope flags a faint moving point near the ecliptic. The player must determine whether it is a real Solar System object, an image artifact, or a known source.

Eleven days before the object passes Earth, the automated survey run by Aino Virtanen has flagged a faint point that moved between three exposures. The same field holds forty thousand catalogued stars, two satellite trails and a column of hot pixels. Today you decide whether there is really an object there, keep the measurements in a state somebody else can use, and say where to point next. Nothing else is known yet — not how big, not what it is made of, not whether this pass is the only one that matters. Every hour of hesitation widens the patch of sky it could be in.
Use digital images, signal-to-noise, artifacts, moving-object detection, controls as an evidence chain rather than as isolated facts.
Object or artifact?
Which explanation fits the motion, image shape, detector map, and independent follow-up?
Survey Telescope Control

The survey software has flagged a faint point that moved between three exposures, in a field holding satellite trails and a hot pixel column. The alert about to go out would task observatories on three continents.
A discovery becomes convincing when motion is coherent in sky coordinates but not tied to one detector, exposure, or telescope.
a detector has its own defects, and they sit still in detector coordinates
The survey software flags a faint moving point near the ecliptic.

A real Solar System object moves in the sky, not on the chip. That is the whole test, and four readings apply it. The source is star-like in every frame, so it is not a cosmic ray, which arrives once and sharp. It lands on different pixels while the background stars stay fixed, so it is not a hot pixel. And a second telescope on another mountain found it near the predicted place — an object that exists for instruments that are not this one.
Real Solar System object
A point source changes sky position coherently while stars and detector coordinates remain stable.
Cosmic-ray hit
A charged particle creates a transient sharp feature in one exposure.
Hot detector pixel
A fixed detector location appears bright whenever that pixel is read.
Frame-alignment artifact
Misalignment makes many fixed stars appear to shift together.
A cosmic ray is a single sharp hit in one exposure. This source is star-like in all three and keeps moving.
A hot pixel is bright wherever that pixel is read, so it stays put in detector coordinates. This one crosses pixels.
An alignment error moves many stars together. Here the stars stay fixed and one point does not.
Validate the discovery
Arrange the four cards from the earliest prerequisite or cause to the latest result. The interface should lock correctly placed cards after each check.
Image Processing Lab
Forty thousand catalogued stars, two satellite trails and a hot pixel column share the frames with the moving point. The pipeline runs tonight in an order somebody will have to defend.
A discovery is useful only when another observer can test it.
a prediction somebody else can test is what makes a claim checkable

Rejection has to come after calibration and before measurement, or every step measures the wrong thing. An uncalibrated frame gives positions that are wrong for instrumental reasons. Measuring before rejecting means astrometry on satellite trails and known asteroids. And the last step is what makes this a discovery rather than a claim: a predicted region hands somebody else a place to point and a way to prove you wrong.
Bias, dark and flat first — positions off an uncalibrated frame are wrong in a way no later step recovers.
Cross-match second: stars, satellites, defects and catalogued objects, or you will measure them very precisely.
Positions and magnitudes third, with uncertainties, because a position without one cannot be fitted to anything.
The ephemeris last, with a region. That is the step that makes this falsifiable by somebody who is not you.
Apply the bias, dark and flat frames, and solve plate constants for each exposure.
Cross-match every source in the field against the star catalogue, the satellite element sets and the defect mask.
Fit positions, magnitudes and per-measurement uncertainties against the observatory clock.
Post an ephemeris with a predicted uncertainty region where another observatory can check it.
How far did it move?
Use the supplied values, show the governing relationship, and give a sensible rounded result with units and interpretation.
Minor-Planet Operations Desk
The object shifted between two frames twenty minutes apart, and the desk has to say where the next telescope should point. Nobody has turned that shift into a rate yet.
Repeated images turn apparent motion into a measurable rate.
a rate is an amount divided by the time it took
Estimate the apparent motion in arcseconds per hour.

Twelve arcseconds in twenty minutes is 0.6 an arcsecond a minute, which is 36 an hour. The 60 in the equation is minutes per hour, so the interval has to be in minutes too. Hand it the same twenty minutes written as 1,200 seconds and the answer comes out sixty times too small — which would look like a main-belt object rather than something close.
The object shifts 12 arcseconds in 20 minutes, and the desk needs a rate before it can predict where to look next.
Estimate the apparent motion in arcseconds per hour.

The 60 in the template is minutes per hour, so the interval has to be in minutes. Handing it the same interval in seconds gives an answer 60 times too small — which would look like a main-belt object rather than something close.
Rate = distance moved ÷ time taken. Multiply by 60 to go from per minute to per hour.
Confirm the Motion
Produce a consistent astrometric track and identify observations that should be down-weighted or repeated.
Follow-up telescopes obtain positions with different clocks and plate solutions. The player must combine astrometry without creating a false trajectory from inconsistent reference frames.

Ten days to the pass, and six observatories have reported positions to Hugo Delacroix, the campaign astrometrist. Two used a different time standard, one recorded no plate solution at all, and one camera's measurements curve away from the orbit fit in a way that looks systematic rather than random. Today you build one clean track out of all of it and buy the next observation. Delacroix will not weight anything down until the room agrees how. A weak track loses the object after the pass, when it will be too faint to find again for years.
Use angular coordinates, plate calibration, time standards, uncertainty, residuals as an evidence chain rather than as isolated facts.
Why do the measured positions disagree?
Which explanation fits the residual pattern across field position, timing, catalog stars, and the independent telescope?
Follow-Up Telescope Network

Astrometry from one wide-field camera curves away from the orbit fit while a second telescope agrees with it. Everything the network has on both is on the screen, and the orbit is due to be published tonight.
An error that tracks the apparatus rather than the target is telling you about the apparatus.
reference stars in the same frame are a control on the frame itself
Follow-up astrometry from one wide-field camera curves away from the orbit fit, while a second telescope agrees.

The reference stars are the control, and they show the same spatial pattern as the asteroid. A residual that follows position on the focal plane belongs to the camera, not to the sky — real acceleration would move the asteroid and leave the stars alone. The timestamps agree with the observatory clock, so it is not timing. A second telescope agrees with the orbit, so it is not the orbit. What is left is the mapping from detector to sky, and the distortion calibration is older than the camera.
Focal-plane distortion calibration error
A position-dependent mapping from detector coordinates to sky coordinates biases both stars and asteroid near the field edge.
Real asteroid acceleration
A physical force changes only the asteroid trajectory on the sky.
Timing error
Incorrect exposure time shifts moving-object positions while fixed reference stars remain correctly mapped.
Catalog-wide star error
The reference catalog is wrong in the same way for both telescopes and all field positions.
Real acceleration acts on the asteroid alone. The reference stars would not follow it, and here they do.
A timing error shifts moving objects and leaves fixed stars correctly placed. Both are displaced here, and the clock checks out.
A catalogue-wide star error would show at the second telescope too, and across the whole field rather than growing toward one edge.
Build the observation arc
Arrange the four cards from the earliest prerequisite or cause to the latest result. The interface should lock correctly placed cards after each check.
Astrometry Lab
Six observatories have reported. Two use a different time standard, one recorded no plate solution at all, and together they cover four hours. The next uncertainty region has to come out of this.
Prediction is the operational test of an astrometric model.
measurements only combine if they are in the same frame and the same clock

Nothing can be fitted across six observatories until every measurement is in one frame and one clock. Mix two time standards and the fit still converges — it just converges on the wrong orbit, and nothing in the residuals says so. Then read the residuals for structure rather than size: scatter is noise, but a pattern that follows one station or one part of a detector is a fault in the instrument. And the output that counts is where the object will be next, because that is the only claim the sky can refute.
Common frame and clock first: two time standards in one fit is an error nobody sees in the residuals afterwards.
A preliminary motion model second — you need something to take residuals against.
Residuals third, and read for structure. Scatter is noise; a pattern following one station is a fault.
The prediction last. The test of an astrometric model is where the object turns up, not how well it fits where it has been.
Place every measurement in a common coordinate and time system.
Fit a preliminary sky-plane motion model.
Inspect residuals for station, time, or field-dependent structure.
State where the object will be on the following night, to the precision a telescope can be pointed with.
Buy the best next observation
Four hours of discretionary time, and the object is faint and setting. What do you book?
Time Standards Room

Four hours of discretionary time on a 2-metre telescope. The object is at magnitude 22.4 and setting two hours after dusk, the arc is four hours long, and the same field is observable again in six nights. A press office has been asking since lunchtime.
The best follow-up is chosen for information gain, not convenience or publicity.
a short arc is consistent with many orbits at once
Four hours of discretionary time, and the object is faint and setting. What do you book?

The orbit family is wide because the arc is short — four hours of a multi-year orbit — and arc length is the quantity that collapses it. Work out what each option adds. A second exposure tonight arrives from nearly the same place in the orbit, so the fit gains a measurement it already effectively has. Parallax constrains distance, which is not what is loose here. Six nights later the object has moved along its path, so the same instrument now measures a genuinely different geometry, and the family of orbits consistent with both points is far narrower. The press release adds no measurement at all.
A later observation that lengthens the time baseline.
Another exposure immediately, from the same telescope.
A geographically separated observation, for parallax.
A press release, before the object is confirmed.
Another exposure tonight adds a measurement almost identical to the ones already held, and identical measurements do not narrow an orbit.
A separated observation adds parallax, which constrains distance rather than arc. It is the right second booking and answers a different question.
A release before confirmation spends the only thing the office cannot buy back, on an object that may not survive the next night.
An Orbit from Sparse Data
Construct a family of allowed orbits and choose observations that collapse the dangerous dimensions.

Only a short arc is available, and many three-dimensional orbits project to nearly the same sky motion. The player must reason with Keplerian motion and orbit families rather than report one overconfident solution.

Nine days to the pass, and the orbit determination lead, Marco Rossi, has stopped quoting a single orbit. Every orbit that fits the observations draws almost the same line across the sky, and they disagree about everything that matters afterwards — this pass is harmless in all of them, and some of them come back in eight years to hit. Today you work out what the data actually pins down and choose the observations that collapse the rest. The single line through the middle is the most dangerous object in this campaign, because it looks like knowledge.
Use Keplerian orbits, state vectors, degeneracy, orbital elements, prediction as an evidence chain rather than as isolated facts.
From angles to orbit family
Arrange the four cards from the earliest prerequisite or cause to the latest result. The interface should lock correctly placed cards after each check.
Orbit Determination Center
Every orbit that fits the arc projects to almost the same track across the sky. Some of them pass a million kilometres from Earth and some do not, and nothing measured so far separates them.
Uncertainty should be carried forward as an ensemble of physically allowed trajectories.
angles alone do not fix a distance

Sparse angular data define a region of state space rather than a single orbit, and the honest procedure is to keep the whole family. Combining the timed directions with any range comes first because range is what angles cannot supply. Generating the states consistent with the observations *and their uncertainties* is what makes it a family rather than a best fit. Each is then carried forward under gravity, and the spread in where they end up is the answer — not the middle of it.
Directions and any range first: a set of angles alone leaves the distance free, which is the dimension the whole problem turns on.
Generate states consistent with the uncertainties, not just the best fit. The best fit is one member of the family and has no special status.
Carry each one forward under gravity — the family has to be carried forward, not the average of it.
Compare the approach distances last. The spread across the family is the result; collapsing it to one number throws the question away.
Combine timed directions and any range information.
Generate state vectors consistent with the observations and uncertainties.
Carry each allowed state forward under gravity.
Compare future sky positions and Earth-approach distances across the family.
Which orbit feature does the data constrain?
Match each part of the orbit to the observation that pins it down. Each choice is used once.
Celestial Mechanics Group
Four kinds of evidence are on offer and the group has to say what each one buys before it spends any telescope time. Each is strong in a different direction.
Orbit determination is an information-geometry problem.
different measurements constrain different parts of an orbit

Orbit determination is an information problem before it is an arithmetic one: what to buy next depends on which direction of the uncertainty is widest. Time is what makes curvature visible, so a longer arc constrains the shape. Radar range fixes that distance directly, as a time of flight. Range rate fixes how fast the distance changes. And two widely separated observers see the object against different backgrounds, which is distance from geometry alone.

Keep observing until the arc is long enough. Over hours the path looks straight, and the curvature that only shows over weeks is what fixes the mean motion, from which Kepler's third law gives the rest.
Take a radar range. The delay of the echo is a time of flight, so multiplying half of it by the speed of light gives the line-of-sight distance to within metres.
Take a radar range rate. The returned frequency is shifted in proportion to the line-of-sight speed, so one echo carries the velocity as well as the distance.

Observe from two widely separated places on Earth at once. The direction to the object differs slightly between the sites, and that parallax angle across a known baseline gives the distance by triangle.
The size and period of an orbit live in how the path curves, and curvature is what time on the sky makes visible.
A distance along the line of sight is a time of flight, which is what a radar echo delivers directly.
How fast that distance is changing is a velocity, and the Doppler shift of the echo is proportional to it.
Two observers far apart see the object against slightly different backgrounds, and that angle with a known baseline is a distance from geometry.
The size and period of the orbit.
The distance to the object right now.
How fast that distance is changing.
A distance from geometry alone, with no orbit assumed.
Collapse the orbit uncertainty
Radar has a window in nine days. What do you do with the nine nights before it?
Follow-Up Scheduling Desk

The allowed orbits form a family, not a line: at Earth's distance they sweep a corridor 40,000 km wide. The arc is eleven hours long, the object fades below the survey limit in twelve nights, and radar has a window in nine days.
A sharper-looking orbit is not a better orbit unless new evidence narrows the allowed family.
an orbit narrows only when new evidence arrives
Radar has a window in nine days. What do you do with the nine nights before it?

Two different things are being traded here, and they are not alternatives. Once the object is beyond reach, the geometry it would have shown has moved on and cannot be revisited, so an unused night is arc lost permanently rather than deferred. Radar, when the window opens, measures range and range rate directly, which optical astrometry never does, and it collapses the corridor by orders of magnitude. But radar has to be pointed, and how well it can be pointed depends on the arc that exists by then. So the nine nights are not a substitute for the radar window; they are what makes it usable.
Extend optical tracking over as many of them as the weather allows.
Hold the telescopes and wait for the radar range.
Observe from a second hemisphere for a parallax baseline.
Reprocess the existing data into a sharper nominal orbit.
Waiting for radar makes the whole campaign depend on one window and one weather forecast, and leaves the arc as short as it is tonight.
A second hemisphere adds parallax where the schedule allows it, and it does not replace the nights of arc that are about to be lost.
A sharper-looking orbit drawn from the same data is the most dangerous product on this list, because it looks like progress and narrows nothing.
The Uncertainty Corridor
Report an impact probability and uncertainty corridor that remain meaningful as new data arrive.

The nominal trajectory misses Earth, but a thin set of allowed solutions passes through it. The player must interpret probability, covariance, and how the spread grows unevenly, without confusing low probability with zero consequence.

Eight days out, and the argument has stopped being about this pass. The best-fit orbit for the return in eight years misses Earth comfortably. A thin set of solutions inside the uncertainty does not, and the corridor they sweep crosses nine million people and a coastline. This morning's numbers moved the impact probability up, and it is already on the wire. Rossi wants to say nothing until the arc is longer. Joan Ellery, who coordinates preparedness for the two counties under the corridor, is right that the number goes public whether or not this room has the words for it. Today you work out that probability properly and decide which observation reduces the uncertainty that is actually driving the number. You get one chance to explain it.
Use probability distributions, covariance, uneven growth of the spread, risk corridors, decision thresholds as an evidence chain rather than as isolated facts.
Read the risk correctly
Match each situation to the most scientifically justified interpretation, control, or response. Each choice is used once.
Impact Monitoring Center
The nominal orbit misses Earth. Four statements about what that does and does not mean are on the board at the monitoring centre, and a press line goes out this afternoon.
Planetary-defense risk lives in the distribution, not just the best-fit trajectory.
a best-fit trajectory is the middle of a distribution, not the whole of it

Risk lives in the distribution of allowed trajectories rather than in the best-fit one, and that has consequences people find counter-intuitive. A nominal miss with allowed solutions passing through Earth is a real risk with a small probability. New data that remove impact solutions lower it legitimately. And probability can *rise* after an observation while the nominal miss distance grows, because shrinking the uncertainty region can concentrate what is left onto Earth. The number moving is not the same as somebody having been wrong.
A miss is not guaranteed while uncertainty remains.
Impact probability is nonzero and should be monitored.
Risk has decreased because the allowed region changed.
Nonlinear geometry can redistribute probability; inspect the full solution set.
A nominal miss is the middle of a distribution. It guarantees nothing while the distribution still reaches Earth.
A thin set of impacting solutions is a nonzero probability, and small is not the same as absent.
Data that remove impact solutions really do lower the risk — that is what the number is for.
A rising probability beside a growing nominal miss is geometry redistributing what is left, not an error.
Nominal orbit misses Earth.
A small fraction of allowed orbits intersect Earth.
New data remove most impact solutions.
Probability rises after an observation even though the nominal miss distance increases.
Probability from an ensemble
Use the supplied values, show the governing relationship, and give a sensible rounded result with units and interpretation.
Statistical Orbit Lab
A simplified Monte Carlo run has finished at the statistical orbit lab. What it produced is a count of samples, and the figure that leaves this room will be quoted in public for years.
A tiny probability can be estimated only with enough samples and a valid uncertainty model.
a probability can be estimated by counting outcomes over trials
Estimate the impact probability, as a percentage.
The figure is only as good as the sampling behind it, and it will be quoted in public long after the assumptions are forgotten.
In a simplified Monte Carlo set, 37 of 100,000 sampled trajectories consistent with the observations strike Earth.
Estimate the impact probability, as a percentage.

The denominator is every sample drawn, not the ones that missed — dividing by the misses gives almost the same number here and the wrong quantity everywhere. A thousand samples could not have resolved a probability this small at all.
Probability = impacting samples ÷ total samples. Multiply by 100 for a percentage.
Reduce the dangerous uncertainty
A thin set of solutions still hits Earth. Where do you point next week?
Planetary Defense Coordination Office

The nominal orbit misses by 4 Earth radii. About 1 in 600 of the solutions inside the uncertainty do not, and next Tuesday those solutions put the object 8 arcseconds from where the rest of the family puts it. Every night after that, the two predictions converge again.
The best observation separates the live hypotheses rather than merely adding another point.
a measurement is informative where the candidate explanations disagree
A thin set of solutions still hits Earth. Where do you point next week?

A measurement is only informative where the live hypotheses disagree. Here that is one night. On Tuesday the impacting solutions and the missing ones sit 8 arcseconds apart, which any follow-up telescope resolves. Before and after, the two families predict the same position within the errors. An observation then is certain to confirm what nobody disputed. So the rule for scheduling follow-up is to point where the predictions diverge, not where the object is brightest — and that condition is a place and a date rather than a telescope.
Where the impacting and non-impacting solutions predict different positions.
Wherever the object is brightest and easiest to measure.
At the same fields again, to improve the astrometric bias calibration.
Nowhere new — run the arc through independent orbit software.
The brightest field is the easiest measurement and the least informative one; every solution already agrees about where the object will be.
Bias calibration improves every measurement a little and separates the two families not at all.
Independent software checks the arithmetic rather than the sky. Worth doing, and it adds no observation.
How Large Is It?
Produce a diameter range rather than a single unsupported value.
The object’s brightness is known, but size depends strongly on reflectivity. The player must combine brightness, albedo, and thermal evidence to bound diameter.

Six days to the pass, and this is the day the campaign has been dreading. Irina Sorokin, who observes in the thermal infrared, has been waiting on telescope time all week. Everything anybody wants to know about the eight-year return scales with size, and the size rests on how bright the object looked in a survey image. Brightness alone allows anything from 120 metres to 600. At the small end this is a city and an evacuation. At the large end it is a country, and a decade of bad harvests for everyone else. Nobody can tell you which, and no amount of staring at the discovery image will. Today you buy the measurement that breaks the tie.
Use brightness, inverse-square law, albedo, thermal emission, size degeneracy as an evidence chain rather than as isolated facts.
What controls apparent brightness?
Match each situation to the most scientifically justified interpretation, control, or response. Each choice is used once.
Photometry Lab
The object was bright enough for a survey telescope to find, and that single number is being read across the room as a size. Four things that change reflected flux are on the board.
A bright asteroid is not necessarily large.
light spreads out with distance

Brightness is the product of all four, which is why the size everybody wants is entangled with a reflectivity nobody has measured. A bigger cross-section reflects more. A more reflective surface reflects more of what arrives. Distance from the Sun sets how much arrives in the first place. Distance from the observer sets how much of what leaves the object reaches the telescope. The same flux comes from a small bright body close in or a large dark one further out.
Usually increases reflected flux.
Increases reflected flux for the same size and geometry.
Reduces illumination.
Reduces received flux through geometric spreading.
A larger cross-section intercepts and returns more light — the term everybody assumes is the only one.
Higher reflectivity returns more of what arrives, at the same size. This is the one that makes brightness ambiguous.
Greater distance from the Sun means less light arriving to be reflected at all.
Greater distance from the observer spreads what does return, so less of it reaches the telescope.
Larger cross-sectional area.
Higher reflectivity.
Greater distance from the Sun.
Greater distance from the observer.
Diameter-albedo degeneracy
Use the supplied values, show the governing relationship, and give a sensible rounded result with units and interpretation.
Infrared Telescope Team
Two objects show the same reflected brightness and one is four times as reflective as the other. The infrared team wants the size comparison written down before anybody quotes a diameter.
Brightness alone cannot uniquely determine size without an albedo assumption.
the area of a disc goes as the square of its diameter
How does the higher-albedo object's diameter compare?

Brightness fixes the product of area and reflectivity. Four times the albedo at the same brightness therefore needs a quarter of the area. But diameter goes as the square root of area, so a quarter of the area is half the diameter, not a quarter of it.
